text: An ecosystem can hold together for a long time and then collapse quite suddenly, once the stress on it crosses a critical load. While the stress stays below that critical load, you see species in decline and only limited extinction cascades. Right at the critical load, those extinction cascades stretch out to become effectively infinite, and species start behaving collectively rather than independently. Push the stress above the critical load and a new, degraded state takes over — one with a qualitatively different pattern of biodiversity loss. Near the critical load the system is exquisitely touchy: a small change in stress can produce a dramatic change in how the ecosystem behaves. This regime shift shows classic collapse dynamics, and strikingly, very different ecosystems display the same critical behavior. Ecologists use resilience theory to predict these collapses and to classify them.

A legislature is made of separate members, and like a pile of grains it can either pour freely or lock into a rigid shape. One number settles which: how far apart the parties have drifted, or polarization. Once that number climbs beyond a particular value, members stop being able to maneuver around each other. Each one is boxed in by the neighbors, and a web of veto alliances, each bearing part of the strain, stretches across the entire chamber. Nobody has become a different person, and nothing has literally frozen or fused together; members have just lost room to rearrange themselves. Even so, the chamber now holds out against pressure for reform with a real, measurable stubbornness, and it will pass nothing until the push exceeds a certain breaking strength. Near the critical value this rigidity is delicate. Strain travels through a thin, branching network of veto alliances, shake-ups arrive as sudden landslides, and a small drop in polarization can melt the whole thing. Students of legislatures care about that critical value because it determines whether the body can still govern and adjust.

Think of a frog-egg extract from Xenopus as resting in one steady phase of the cell cycle while its level of cyclin B stays below a key trigger level. When cyclin B reaches that trigger, even slight further changes in its amount sharply rewire the interplay between Cdk1, the kinase that drives division, Cdc25, the phosphatase that switches it on, and Wee1, the kinase that holds it off. The extract then flips into another cell-cycle phase marked by its own pattern of mitosis-specific phosphate tags on proteins. As the extract nears the trigger, it responds more and more sluggishly, and the swings in Cdk1 activity grow larger and larger. Across the switch, Cdk1 activity jumps abruptly, or the rate at which it changes shoots off without bound. In the new phase, a pattern of mitotic phosphate tagging appears that simply did not exist in the earlier phase. The switch often shows memory: the cyclin B level at which it flips depends on whether cyclin B is rising or falling. Systems biologists investigate how the large-scale pattern of mitotic phosphate tagging arises from the small-scale interactions among Cdk1, Cdc25, and Wee1 near this trigger level.

Consider a film of algae coating the bottom of a temporary pond, shared by many wood frog tadpoles that each turn it into growth. Because the film is not divided up among them, every tadpole is tempted to scrape as much of it as it can, even though this may use up the food for all of them. The price of that shortage, a later change into froglets, is spread over the whole group, while the faster growth from scraping goes to the single tadpole that did it. That sets up a contest in which sensible behavior by each tadpole adds up to a stunted age group that makes no sense for the whole. To stop the algal film from being used up, tadpoles must directly hinder one another, which holds the scraping down and ties each tadpole's interest to the algae staying productive over the long run. Amphibian ecology looks at how tadpoles handle this contest and how well such direct hindering works.

Think of the people who give to political campaigns as a lake with a limited amount of water, and every candidate fishing in it. Each candidate wants as much money for their own campaign as possible, so they send more and more email asks to the same supporters. The money raised from those extra emails goes only to the candidate who sent them, but the weariness of the recipients as the lake is drawn down is felt by every candidate. So each candidate is tempted to send too many, and eventually supporters tune out entirely. Once the lake is dry, every candidate sees their donations shrink sharply. To prevent this drying up of supporters, party rules or shared fundraising efforts are needed to keep the asks in check and preserve supporters' interest over the long run. Campaign studies looks at how candidates handle this dilemma and at how well different limits on how often emails go out perform.

A single host cell holds several copies of a plasmid, and every copy benefits from living inside it by being passed along within the cell. Since they all occupy the cell together, each copy is pushed to replicate as fast as possible, even if the cell then grows poorly for everyone. The cost to host fitness from that slowed growth falls on all the copies, while the gain in transmission from faster replication belongs to the single copy that made it. That sets up selection acting on more than one level, and sensible choices by each copy add up to a result nobody would choose: runaway copy numbers. To keep the cell from dying, there must be limits on how many copies it carries, holding down replication and bringing each copy's interest in line with the lasting survival of the cell. Plasmid biology studies how copies handle this layered selection and how well different copy-number limits work.

An Allenby's gerbil can predict that its moonlit foraging bout will find it in a heated frame of mind: hungry, exposed to owls, and with seeds seemingly just a bit further on. It also knows that whatever it concludes in that moment will be its poorest thinking. So it settles the matter earlier, while things are quiet. In the calm period before, it picks a giving-up density and agrees with itself that when the seed supply in a patch drops to that level, it will leave right then and not stop to think it over again. Once the bout is underway, the gerbil no longer wonders whether it ought to leave; its only question is whether the giving-up density has been hit. This rule can err on the side of safety and make the gerbil abandon seeds that could in fact have been collected without danger. Yet it dependably guards against being struck by an owl, a much bigger loss, which usually comes out of lingering too long in a patch, driven by the belief that this one time staying is warranted. Optimal foraging theory holds that a giving-up density is of no use unless it is fixed ahead of the moonlit bout and kept without any bargaining.

Standing in front of the voters, a lawmaker formally promises to vote against any tax hike, well aware that if the choice were left to private calculation, plenty of reasons to raise taxes would turn up later. Signing the anti-tax promise alters almost nothing in the real world except what everyone now expects of the lawmaker, but that turns out to be plenty: from that day on, any vote for higher taxes would be noticed and recalled as going back on one's word, and the lawmaker's standing as a conservative would take the hit. The louder and more precise the promise, the more expensive any quiet deal on taxes becomes, so the lawmaker phrases it so that no clever reading can wriggle around it, and puts it in writing with a signature, so it lasts long after the enthusiasm of the moment has faded. When the budget later comes up short, the lawmaker finds that the real choice was settled long ago, on the day the promise was signed; the only thing still undecided is whether the public will watch the lawmaker vote for higher taxes. Scholars of political messaging look at how statements that are cheap to make can become very expensive to go back on.

A somatic cell lineage begins clonal growth with the understanding that the safest time to set its stopping point is before division starts. Late in this expansion, growth signals make each additional division seem inexpensive, DNA-damage sites seem tolerable, and further tissue growth appear close at hand. The lineage therefore establishes a critical telomere length beforehand, using telomere length as an honest measure, and stops clonal growth once that threshold is crossed. This limit works because it was selected before immediate pressures arose and cannot be revised later; if growth signals could shift it, it would be merely advisory. Occasionally, the lineage gives up tissue growth even though another division might have worked, but this protects it from genomic crisis in the many cases where continued division would fail. In senescence biology, critical telomere length allows the unpressured lineage at the outset to control the growth-driven lineage near the end.

Un ensemble de populations de daphnies garde le rythme : chaque population de daphnies suit son propre cycle naturel d'explosion et d'effondrement, et ces périodes naturelles diffèrent légèrement d'une population à l'autre. Par la dispersion le long des cours d'eau, chaque population pousse les autres vers sa propre phase. Tant que la dispersion est faible, c'est la diversité qui l'emporte : chaque population dérive à son allure, les phases se dispersent, et la biomasse régionale se moyenne en un niveau presque sans relief. Renforcer la dispersion ne change rien de visible jusqu'à ce qu'elle atteigne une force critique. Alors un petit noyau de populations dont la période naturelle est proche du milieu de la distribution se cale ensemble ; son attraction combinée capte des populations un peu plus éloignées, ce qui renforce encore l'attraction, et une pulsation régionale commune émerge du bruit. La force critique appartient à l'ensemble des populations, non à l'un de ses membres : plus l'écart entre périodes naturelles est large, plus la dispersion doit être forte pour le surmonter. Juste au-dessus de la force critique, le noyau calé agit comme un seul amas de lacs tandis que les populations les plus déviantes dérivent encore à l'extérieur ; plus haut, le noyau les absorbe presque toutes. Si l'on affaiblit de nouveau la dispersion, la pulsation régionale commune se dissout en fluctuations indépendantes. L'écologie des métacommunautés modélise l'apparition de ce phénomène par un seul nombre, le degré de cohérence de phase entre les populations de daphnies, qui, dans le modèle standard, croît continûment à partir de zéro dès que la dispersion dépasse la force critique.
